crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Judicial Analytics
children.blurb: Judicial analytics is the study of courts, judges, and litigation outcomes using data and computational methods.

children.name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
children.blurb: Opposing counsel and docket patterns is the study of how lawyers and courts behave across the life of a case, using public filings to see what each side tends to file, when, and with what result.

children.name: Settlement Valuation and Risk
children.blurb: Settlement valuation and risk is the practice of estimating the likely financial terms of a civil settlement and the probability of various outcomes if a dispute proceeds to trial or arbitration.

children.name: Jury Selection and Public Data
children.blurb: Jury selection and public data covers the use of open records, such as voter files, property rolls, court dockets, and campaign finance filings, to build profiles of people in a jury pool.

children.name: Live Testimony Cross-Referencing
children.blurb: Live testimony cross-referencing applies automated comparison to spoken witness evidence as it is given, checking it against prior depositions, affidavits, exhibits, and other testimony already in the case record.

sections.body: Litigation prediction and judicial analytics is the use of court records, dockets, briefs, rulings, transcripts, verdicts, and public data to estimate how a case, a judge, a jury, or an opponent may behave. In practice, AI systems now read and classify large document sets, extract parties and claims, track procedural deadlines, and surface patterns across thousands of matters. They can compare a judge's past rulings on similar motions, flag inconsistencies in deposition or trial testimony, and build rough settlement ranges from historical outcomes. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which gives this section a live and still small body of material to study. The work is not a crystal ball. It is a set of statistical and retrieval tools that depend on the quality and completeness of the underlying record.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are mature. Docket monitoring, document review, citation checking, and basic outcome statistics work well at scale, and AI can reliably find prior statements that conflict with live testimony. Other parts remain hard. Predicting the result of a specific case is unreliable because facts, witnesses, judges, juries, and law change, and because many settlements and jury deliberations are not public. Models trained on past decisions can reproduce historical bias, and they cannot see sealed filings, private negotiations, or a judge's unstated reasoning. Validation is difficult, so a probability score is a summary of patterns, not a verdict. The 29 AI case law precedents on the site show that courts are still building doctrine around AI evidence and analytics, which limits how much can be generalized.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader can begin with Judicial Analytics to see how a judge's history, written opinions, and motion rulings are turned into profiles. Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns follows the other side, looking at filing habits, procedural moves, and timing across matters. Settlement Valuation and Risk connects those patterns to ranges, exposure, and uncertainty, while Jury Selection and Public Data examines what public records can and cannot say about a jury pool. Live Testimony Cross-Referencing is the page for the courtroom, where transcripts and prior statements are compared in real time to support examination and impeachment. Together these pages move from the bench, to the opponent, to the money, to the jury, and finally to the live words spoken in court.
